title: Five Practices from My 1980s Elementary School That Should Make a Comeback
author: Ayaan Hirsi Ali Source: restoringthewest.com
summary: Responding to 2025 Gallup data showing that only 41% of Gen Z adults are extremely or very proud to be American — compared to 83% of the Silent Generation — Ayaan Hirsi Ali argues that American schools must deliberately transmit civic pride and republican values, and draws on five practices from her own 1980s elementary education as a model. The five practices are: daily recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance as an embodied reminder of national unity; memorization and recitation of key founding texts (the Preamble, Declaration of Independence) so those principles are carried in long-term memory; use of music class to teach patriotic songs from the E.D. Hirsch cultural literacy canon; ceremonial flag duty instilling reverence and civic responsibility; and collective school-wide marking of shared national moments. The underlying premise — following Noah Webster (1788) and Ronald Reagan — is that freedom and republican self-government must be actively transmitted to each generation through education, since they are not automatically inherited.
points: Only 41% of Gen Z adults are extremely or very proud to be American versus 83% of the Silent Generation — a Gallup 2025 finding Hirsi Ali treats as evidence of a generation-long failure of civic transmission in American schools.

Daily Pledge of Allegiance recitation provides a concrete, embodied reminder that 'despite our differences, we are One nation under God' — an experience of shared identity that transcends political division.
Memorizing key founding texts carries those principles into students' long-term memory 'long after the lesson ends,' achieving a durability no worksheet or textbook reading can match.

'Flag duty' — being chosen to raise and lower Old Glory — instilled civic responsibility and reverence in a way 'no textbook lesson could fully replicate,' creating ownership of a symbol rather than passive exposure to it.
Reagan's framing undergirds the piece: freedom 'is not ours by way of inheritance; it must be fought for and defended constantly by each generation, for it comes only once to a people.'

When students commit these words to memory, they carry the principles of the American founding with them long after the lesson ends.

Being entrusted with raising or lowering Old Glory, as well as proper flag etiquette, was a reminder that the flag stands for something bigger than itself — something worth honoring. That small ritual instilled a sense of civic responsibility and respect that no textbook lesson could fully replicate.
